candidateRows: Consciousness should be treated as reality's foundation because it is the sole pre-theoretical given to which a parsimonious reduction can appeal.
This establishes the affirmative's foundational ontology and its governing criterion of reducing nature to consciousness as the only immediate datum.
In answering the opening question, Kastrup presents consciousness as the starting point prior to theory and argues that ontological parsimony favors reducing reality's complexity to it.
Strong emergence from a nonconscious substrate is explanatorily empty, while idealism is preferable if it can preserve an objective and scientifically tractable world.
The move rejects the motion's principal emergentist alternative and states the empirical adequacy condition that Kastrup believes idealism must satisfy.
The moderator's suggestion that consciousness might be intrinsic to, or emergent from, physical processes.

Kastrup argues that physical quantities cannot entail experiential qualities, characterizes strong emergence as semantically ungrounded, and conditions idealism's superiority on explaining objective science.
Rejecting matter-to-consciousness emergence does not establish analytic idealism, whose dissociation account fails to explain why the world has its observed structure.
This articulates the negative's central distinction between sharing the critique of materialist emergence and accepting Kastrup's specifically idealist ontology.
Kastrup's claim that evidence against emergence and representational physicality makes analytic idealism the best available hypothesis.

Blackmore agrees that standard consciousness studies wrongly seek an extra property generated by brains, but argues that Kastrup's alter-based dissociation analogy supplies no account of cosmic order.
Analytic idealism permits a mind-independent external world whose inaccessible mental states are represented to observers as the physical world.
The move supplies the affirmative's core reconciliation of idealism with objectivity, observer independence, perception, and the apparent existence of physical reality.
Blackmore's objection that idealism lacks an explanation of an ordered external world and appears unable to distinguish it from private experience.

Kastrup distinguishes private perceptual qualities from external mental states, comparing perception to an instrument dashboard that represents a real observer-independent world without making it physical in itself.
Calling the inaccessible substrate mental adds no explanatory content unless idealism explains the boundary, machinery, and structured predictive representations involved.
This targets whether the affirmative's ontological relabeling performs explanatory work rather than merely avoiding the terminology associated with physicalism.
Kastrup's account of an inaccessible external mental world represented through perception as an apparently physical world.
Blackmore argues that representationalism still requires an account of the substrate producing structured predictions and asks what explanatory benefit follows from designating that substrate mental.
Dissociation can generate embodied boundaries within a universal mental reality, while natural selection and stable dispositions preserve ordinary causal science and physical predictability.
This answers the demand for a boundary mechanism and explains how idealism can accommodate biology, evolution, physical laws, regular causation, and non-anthropomorphic order.
Blackmore's challenge to identify what separates internal from external mental states and why a mental world exhibits structured physical regularities.

Kastrup treats skin and sensory interfaces as appearances of dissociative boundaries, places replicating dissociations under natural selection, and portrays external mentality as automatic and disposition-governed rather than deliberative.
The hard problem can be avoided through neutral monism by locating what-it-is-like in representations rather than in a separately presumed physical organism.
This presents the negative's positive neutral-monist alternative, intended to avoid the hard problem without adopting consciousness as the universal ontological substance.
Kastrup's contention that only idealism can remove the hard problem while retaining subjective experience and an objective world.
Blackmore argues that moving from what experience is like to a physical bat creates the hard problem; restricting the claim to a bat's self-representation dissolves the mistaken transition.
Representational self-models can dissolve the personal agent, but materialist illusionism still presupposes experience and therefore cannot eliminate consciousness.
The move concedes the constructed self while defending consciousness itself as irreducible, thereby distinguishing idealism from materialist illusionism at the debate's central fault line.
Blackmore's proposal that phenomenal character belongs only to representational models and that this move avoids entering the hard problem.

Kastrup agrees that enduring agents are delusive mental models, but argues that a materialist hierarchy of models merely repeats the explanatory gap and that experienced illusions require consciousness.
If phenomenal character belongs to representations, then even fleeting low-level models may have something it is like to be them independently of an ephemeral self-model.
This extends the negative's representational neutral monism into an account of distributed phenomenal character that does not privilege a unified or persistent personal self.
Kastrup's inference that the experience of delusive self-models supports consciousness-only idealism rather than a broader representational account.

Blackmore proposes a qualified panpsychism of representations across processing levels, arguing that experience continues among multiple models when meditation or psychedelics dissolve the organizing self-model.
Integrated information theory supports subjective viewpoints outside the narrative self because maximal complexes exclude states that remain independently integrated mental processes.
The bounded concluding move supplies a formal mechanism for consciousness beyond the ego and connects distributed experience to Kastrup's idealist interpretation of mental complexes.
Blackmore's claim that low-level and non-self representations retain phenomenal character even when they are not incorporated into the personal self-model.

Kastrup invokes IIT's maximal complexes and fault lines to explain how integration can increase by excluding states, while excluded complexes retain their own subjective perspectives outside the narrative self.
Integrated information theory does not explain why information integration entails any subjective experience at all.
The challenge presses the explanatory gap between measurable integration and phenomenal consciousness, directly testing whether the theory supports the motion.
Bernardo's claim that IIT complexes necessarily possess subjective points of view.
After Bernardo connects IIT complexes with subjective perspectives outside the narrative self, Susan asks why greater integration should mean consciousness exists in greater degree.
At its operational level, IIT maps measurable brain states to reported experience without itself constituting a metaphysical theory.
The distinction limits what empirical IIT must explain while preserving its usefulness for inferring consciousness from measurable physical states.
Susan's challenge that IIT fails to explain why integrated information is conscious.
Bernardo responds that IIT first functions as a predictive bridge between brain activity and subjective reports, including cases where reports are unavailable.
IIT's account of causation modestly favors idealism because only experiential complexes exist for themselves and possess causal power.
The argument links causal existence to experience and therefore supplies direct support for consciousness, rather than nonexperiential matter, as ontologically basic.
Susan's request for clarification about what IIT says consciousness is and why it exists.

Bernardo distinguishes representational objects from self-existing complexes, argues that only the latter cause anything, and concludes that this structure leans toward idealism without strictly implying it.
Invoking a dreaming subject as the cause of an imagined object is problematic when the self itself lacks clear or stable existence.
The objection challenges the causal unit on which Bernardo's interpretation depends, questioning whether his account merely presupposes the contested self.
Bernardo's claim that the dreaming complex causes the imagined elephant while the elephant causes nothing.
Susan accepts the example's relevance but asks what the causal first-person subject could be after both speakers have treated ordinary selves as constructed or misleading.
Experiences are excitations of one universal core subjectivity rather than separate contents generated by individual material subjects.
The account directly identifies the underlying reality with subjectivity and treats every particular experience and apparent individual as a mode of that foundation.
Susan's objection that the supposed dream-causing self is unclear once personal selves are treated as constructions.
Bernardo moves beyond operational IIT, distinguishes subjectivity from its particular excitations, and proposes a single core subjectivity whose modes comprise everything else.
Dreams without an experienced self leave idealism and IIT without a clear account of where causal differentiation originates.
The challenge targets whether a consciousness-first ontology can explain causal distinctions inside experience without relying on a separate personal agent.
Bernardo's account of a universal subjectivity whose experiential complex causes dream imagery.
Susan contrasts deliberate waking imagery with ordinary nonlucid dreams, where no clear self appears, and asks what causes one dream element rather than another.
Causality arises from the intrinsic archetypal properties and natural excitation modes of the single universal field of subjectivity.
The explanation supplies the proposed consciousness-first ontology with an internal source of causal order, differentiation, and emergent natural complexity.
Susan's demand for the source of causality and differentiation within dreams lacking an apparent personal self.
Bernardo argues that universal subjectivity must self-excite according to inherent properties, using harmonics and simple emergent rules to explain structured complexity.
Meditative experience in which events persist without ordinary time or space raises doubt that spacetime is fundamental.
The observation challenges any ontology that assumes spacetime while asking whether altered consciousness provides evidence for a more fundamental neutral basis.
Bernardo's field analogy and acknowledgment that contemporary physics may treat spacetime as nonfundamental.
Susan describes open-eye meditative states containing ongoing experience without ordinary spatial or temporal organization and asks Bernardo how to understand them.
Idealism explains nonspatial and nontemporal natural structure as semantic or cognitive structure grounded in meaning.
The argument claims a distinctive explanatory advantage for idealism by grounding structured reality in cognition when spatial and temporal extension are absent.
Susan's question whether experiences outside ordinary space and time indicate that spacetime is not fundamental.
Bernardo reviews the problem of differentiation without extension, rejects ungrounded mathematical abstraction, and proposes meaning-bearing cognitive relations as extension-independent structure.
